responses.strategic_rationale: This residential parasomnia research unit navigates three fundamental tensions: (1) capturing infrequent, naturalistic events while maintaining participant safety and comfort in a domestic setting; (2) balancing operational simplicity and staff safety across 8 suites with clinical-grade neurophysiological rigor; and (3) proving the facility's scientific value within a constrained 36-month window and finite €3.8M budget. The selected levers address recruitment reliability, staffing resilience, sensor data quality and annotation burden, event-capture yield optimization, and stakeholder alignment — each directly affecting the core probability of reaching the 50–70 participant and 40-event thresholds that determine funding survival and publication viability.

levers.name: Recruitment pathway stringency and bed-partner corroboration
levers.consequences: Stricter pre-admission clinical assessment and mandatory bed-partner history validation reduce enrollment velocity but increase likelihood that admitted participants actually produce parasomnia events during their stay, raising event-capture yield and reducing unproductive admissions. Conversely, looser intake criteria accelerate participant throughput but risk admitting non-event-producing individuals who consume facility time and staff attention without contributing to Aim 2 phenotyping or Aim 3 algorithm benchmarking.
options: Require prospective event logs and actigraphy tracings for 4 weeks prior to admission, with bed-partner structured interview conducted by the clinical psychologist before consent, adjudicated by the PI to confirm ≥2 episodes per month with documented witness accounts

Implement single-night screening polysomnography in the university hospital sleep lab before residential unit admission, using standard AASM criteria to confirm parasomnia events or high-arousal burden, accepting longer pre-admission latency but filtering out misdiagnosed referrals

Accept specialist clinical referral and patient self-report with brief telephone bed-partner screening, prioritizing enrollment speed over pre-admission event confirmation and tolerating a higher proportion of non-productive admissions that trigger extended-stay protocols or contribute to the 20% unproductive threshold
levers.review_lever: Stricter screening slows enrollment but increases event yield; looser screening sacrifices yield for speed — the options do not address how to recover lost participants if screening backlog exceeds PI capacity or if regional referral networks deplete before enrollment targets are reached.

levers.name: Night technician staffing model and shift coverage
levers.consequences: The current plan deploys 3 technicians rotating night shifts to cover 8 active suites. A dedicated 4-person roster with overlap increases margin for event response, real-time annotation accuracy, and staff fatigue management, but adds €80K–€120K annually in salaries plus social insurance. Conversely, outsourcing night coverage to a contracted nursing agency trades salary burden for reduced control over annotation quality, event-flagging consistency, and participant relationship continuity.
options: Hire a fourth technician to implement a 4-on-3-off rotating roster with one technician free for ad-hoc escalation or annotation spillover, absorbing the additional cost as a priority within personnel budget to sustain annotation throughput and participant safety margins at full 8-suite capacity

Negotiate a contracted night-nursing partnership with a local Bonn agency under a protocol-specific training agreement, where agency staff complete a 2-week facility orientation and follow standardized event-flagging and annotation workflows, reducing fixed payroll but introducing turnover risk and potential annotation drift

Operate the 3-person roster at full capacity with a documented protocol ceiling of 6 active suites at any time to manage technician workload within safe limits, accepting slower enrollment velocity and longer study duration but avoiding overstaffing cost if participant recruitment remains below target.
levers.review_lever: Hiring a fourth technician secures annotation quality and safety margin but locks in fixed cost; outsourcing reduces payroll but risks annotation drift; capping suites at 6 avoids overstaffing cost but conflicts with the 50–70 participant enrollment target if sustained recruitment exceeds 6-suite capacity.

levers.name: Dry-electrode EEG headband reliability and backup sensing strategy
levers.consequences: The tiered acquisition model uses dry-electrode EEG headbands for nightly low-burden monitoring, reducing participant discomfort and improving compliance, but dry-electrode contact quality degrades over multi-week stays and can produce motion artifacts during parasomnia events. A contingency strategy — such as maintaining a spare headband inventory and training technicians in real-time contact troubleshooting — mitigates data-loss risk but requires procedural discipline. Relying entirely on scheduled enhanced-night PSG (first, mid, final nights) as backup may miss events occurring on other nights.
options: Stock a 2-week rotating spare headband inventory with standardized contact-gel resupply and train technicians to perform contact-quality checks and in-situ electrode replacement during each morning review window, treating headband maintenance as a core daily task and budgeting for incremental gel and replacement-electrode costs

Deploy full standard scalp EEG (10–20 system) every night rather than reserving it for enhanced nights, accepting increased setup labor and participant discomfort but eliminating the risk that infrequent events on non-enhanced nights are captured only by low-resolution contact-free sensors

Use dry-electrode headbands nightly with no backup EEG on non-enhanced nights, relying on contact-free mattress sensors, infrared video, and microphone data to detect parasomnia episodes and escalate to full PSG setup after technician-flagged events, accepting the tradeoff that initial event morphology on non-enhanced nights remains low-resolution unless escalation occurs.
levers.review_lever: Headband maintenance adds procedural overhead and consumable cost; nightly full scalp EEG increases setup labor and participant burden; pure low-resolution reliance gambles on escalation-flag accuracy — none address how to recover or retrospectively analyze morphology if a headband fails mid-event on a non-enhanced night.

levers.name: Event-triage algorithm development scope and human-scorer dependency
levers.consequences: The plan commits to semi-automated event-triage tools benchmarked against dual human scorer agreement, reducing manual review burden (Aim 3) while preserving clinical rigor. Expanding the algorithm to autonomously diagnose parasomnia subtype (sleepwalking vs. terror vs. confusional arousal) requires larger training datasets and validation complexity, risking missed publication deadline if algorithm development extends into year three. Conversely, limiting the algorithm to event-presence detection only (binary: parasomnia vs. background motion) reduces development scope but provides less actionable output for clinical phenotyping.
options: Scope the algorithm to detect parasomnia event windows and rank confidence, leaving human scorers to classify subtype and morphology, completing algorithm benchmarking by month 24 and publishing Aim 3 results within the grant timeline

Design the algorithm to classify NREM parasomnia subtype (sleepwalking vs. confusional arousal vs. terror) using multi-modal sensor features and video motion signatures, accepting extended development timeline and deferring final benchmarking to month 30–32 with Aim 3 publication contingent on timely data accumulation

Restrict the algorithm to detecting gross nocturnal movement above a static threshold (e.g., mattress pressure and video motion exceeding baseline), deliberately avoiding subtype classification or morphological analysis, completing a lightweight tool by month 18 that supports technician workflow but offers minimal novel scientific content for publication.
levers.review_lever: Full subtype classification risks timeline slippage; binary detection alone limits publication novelty; hybrid scope still requires dual human scoring for algorithm ground truth, leaving the resource burden of training and retaining two independent raters unaddressed.

levers.name: Matched control cohort size and recruitment source
levers.consequences: The plan includes a matched control group to benchmark sensor false-positive rates and normal nocturnal movement patterns. Recruiting 20–25 matched controls (matched on age, sex, BMI) in parallel with patient enrollment provides robust baselines for Aim 3 algorithm specificity. Conversely, recruiting controls sequentially after patient enrollment completes eliminates resource contention but delays algorithm validation. Recruiting controls from the general population (e.g., via university advertisement) is faster than recruiting from the hospital but may miss sleep-clinic workers or staff who have high familiarity with the facility and atypical sleep patterns.
options: Enroll 20–25 matched controls on the same recruitment timeline as parasomnia patients, assigning controls to 1–2 dedicated suite rotations per month and training technicians in control-specific workflows (shorter stays, simpler consent, absence of event-escalation protocols), to complete algorithm specificity benchmarking in parallel with patient data collection

Recruit matched controls exclusively from University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic staff and immediate family members, leveraging convenience sampling and pre-existing trust but accepting potential bias if clinic workers have altered sleep physiology due to occupational stress or shift work history

Defer control recruitment to months 28–32 after achieving the target 50–70 parasomnia participants, allowing full focus on event capture during the main study window and performing algorithm specificity analysis in a compressed timeline with parallel control stays.
levers.review_lever: Parallel control enrollment adds recruitment burden and suite allocation pressure during year one; convenience sampling from clinic staff risks physiological bias; deferring controls simplifies year-one operations but compresses algorithm validation into months 28–32, creating timeline risk if data quality review or rater retraining is needed.

levers.name: Data sharing repository selection and privacy-constraint communication
levers.consequences: The plan designates public data sharing to de-identified physiological and sensor data only, excluding bedroom video due to privacy constraints. Depositing data in a specialized sleep-research repository (e.g., NATDB, OpenNeuro, SleepData.org) maximizes discoverability and reproducibility but requires BIDS compliance enforcement and licensing agreements negotiation. Alternatively, restricting data sharing to collaborator-requested access under formal data use agreements reduces public burden but limits discoverability and reproducibility. Clear communication to participants about video-non-sharing increases trust and consent robustness.
options: Commit to depositing de-identified polysomnography, dry-electrode headband, mattress-sensor, and environmental-sensor streams in OpenNeuro Sleep using EEG-BIDS formatting, with dual-anonymization (remove dates, replace identifiers) and automatic flagging of video-containing sessions as excluded from deposition, completing deposit within 3 months of final publication to maximize discoverability

Implement a restricted-access model where polysomnography and sensor data are shared only to qualified sleep researchers under formal data use agreements signed with the university legal office, allowing fine-grained control over reuse but requiring a data-sharing coordinator role and accepting reduced public impact compared to open-repository deposition

Create a study-specific data portal hosted on University of Bonn servers with conditional access to de-identified streams, where external researchers submit a research proposal and gain access within 2 weeks if approved by the PI, striking a middle ground between discoverability and privacy control but introducing administrative overhead and portal maintenance.
levers.review_lever: OpenNeuro deposition maximizes reproducibility but requires strict BIDS compliance and early commitment; restricted data-use agreements preserve privacy control but require dedicated coordination; a university portal balances control and access but depends on sustained IT infrastructure and governance, leaving the long-term maintenance burden unspecified.

levers.name: Year-two expansion decision trigger and facility utilization threshold
levers.consequences: The plan defers 4-suite expansion (from 8 to 12 active suites) until pilot data confirms acceptable data quality, false-alarm rates, and staffing safety by the end of year one. Expanding early maximizes enrollment velocity and event-yield accumulation toward the 50–70 target, but risks operational chaos if staffing or annotation infrastructure is unprepared. Deferring expansion entirely protects year-two cash flow and reduces risk of over-capacity chaos, but may result in undershoot of enrollment targets if year-one recruitment outpaces pilot projections.
options: Trigger expansion to 12 suites in month 13 if year-one data achieves ≥80% suite utilization (i.e., ≥6.4 suites occupied on average), ≥70% event-capture rate (participants producing ≥1 adjudicated event), and inter-rater reliability ≥0.75 kappa for parasomnia event classification, with facility director and external SAB approval required before hiring expansion staff

Commit to 8-suite cap through month 24 regardless of year-one recruitment success, prioritizing operational stability and staff learning-curve maturation over enrollment velocity, with a formal go/no-go review in month 20 assessing whether event-yield and publication progress warrant expansion planning for month 25 onward

Conduct a month-12 capacity utilization audit and automatically scale staffing (but not physical suites) to 4-person technician roster and enhanced-night PSG frequency if average suite occupancy exceeds 7 suites, deferring physical suite expansion until month 18 when renovations can be planned and contracted, maintaining flexibility while protecting year-one operations.
levers.review_lever: Quantitative expansion triggers reduce subjective decision-making but assume month-13 staffing availability and reinforce suite-utilization dependency; 8-suite cap prioritizes stability but risks enrollment shortfall if word-of-mouth recruitment accelerates; scaled staffing without suite expansion buys time but still commits to additional hiring before physical expansion certainty.

responses.strategic_rationale: This early-stage clinical research facility must navigate three fundamental tensions: capturing rare, naturalistic parasomnia events while maintaining domestic, non-clinical conditions that suppress behavioral suppression; recruiting and safely housing participants with nocturnal movement disorders across a 3-year horizon with constrained budget and staffing; and developing actionable event-triage tools without over-promising autonomous diagnosis or falling into manual-scoring bottlenecks. The selected levers address sequencing of facility ramp-up, participant dwell-time management, technician workload sustainability, algorithm validation rigor, external funding dependency, and institutional embedding—each pressuring operational capacity or scientific credibility against the other.

levers.name: Participant dwell-time architecture and re-admission protocols
levers.consequences: Choosing between longer single stays (2–8 weeks, or extended to 10 weeks for zero-event cases) versus repeated shorter admissions (e.g., two 2-week stays separated by months) directly affects event capture likelihood but creates different staffing load curves and participant burden. Longer stays may improve within-person temporal clustering detection but increase accommodation risk; shorter repeated stays distribute risk but require re-consent, re-baseline, and repeated technician orientation, multiplying annotation overhead.
options: Implement a fixed 4-week baseline stay for all participants with a structured optional second admission triggered only if zero events are captured during the first stay, capping total facility exposure time per participant at 8 weeks and creating a stable scheduling pattern.

Deploy an adaptive stay-length model in which initial stay duration (2–5 weeks) is set by the PI after pre-admission assessment of episode frequency history, with post-stay event-count data driving individual re-admission decisions within the 10-week ceiling, optimizing for high event-yield per participant but requiring continuous real-time scheduling recalculation.

Offer all participants a structured three-visit protocol of two separate 2-week admissions separated by 4–6 weeks at home, bookended by a final 1-week validation stay, enabling longitudinal within-person variance assessment and comparison of home versus residential capture but requiring tripled consent and technician cross-training cycles.
levers.review_lever: Longer stays improve event capture per admission but create seasonal staffing peaks and participant fatigue-driven safety risks; shorter repeated stays distribute load but triple administrative overhead and inter-rater consistency challenges across separate baseline periods.

levers.name: Technician shift-rotation stability and on-call surge capacity
levers.consequences: The unit currently plans 3 rotating technicians covering 8 active suites per night with margin for event response and real-time annotation. Choosing between a fixed roster of permanent full-time technicians versus a hybrid model mixing core staff with per-shift on-call contractors or regional sleep center partnerships determines long-term cost stability, annotation consistency, and continuity of participant safety protocols. Permanent staff ensures protocol fidelity and builds institutional memory but locks in fixed wages; hybrid models provide budget flexibility and surge capacity for year-two expansion but introduce training variability and annotation drift.
options: Maintain a stable core of 3 full-time permanent technicians supplemented by a pre-qualified on-call freelance pool from regional sleep centers, staggered to cover unplanned absences and participant surges, with quarterly cross-training sessions and spot-check dual-annotation alignment audits.

Hire 4 permanent full-time technicians from year one, creating intentional redundancy for participant safety and enabling one dedicated technician per 2 suites on each shift, accepting higher baseline labor costs but achieving superior continuity of scoring methodology and participant rapport.

Contract with a specialized overnight staffing agency to supply technicians on a per-shift basis, supplemented by a single dedicated full-time facility manager who orients each temporary technician and audits annotation quality, minimizing facility fixed costs but outsourcing consistency and requiring robust quality-control infrastructure.
levers.review_lever: Permanent staff ensures consistency but locks in fixed wages regardless of utilization; hybrid and agency models trade flexibility for training overhead and inter-rater drift that compounds annotation bottlenecks.

levers.name: Facility safety-incident response threshold and escalation authority
levers.consequences: Adults with parasomnia carry inherent nocturnal movement and confusion risk—the facility design mitigates via padded corridors and door alarms, but decisions about when to restrict admissions, call emergency services, extend monitoring, or exclude participants from further stays shape both safety perception and recruitment continuity. A strict incident-response protocol with low thresholds (e.g., immediate psychiatric consultation after any participant confusion or injury, mandatory emergency department evaluation) protects liability but may deter participant re-admission and create false-positive safety exclusions; permissive thresholds maximize enrollment but increase reputational and medical risk.
options: Establish a strict incident-escalation protocol requiring immediate notification to the clinical psychologist, documentation in a safety event log, and structured psychiatric clearance or exclusion before any participant returns for a subsequent stay, prioritizing transparency and institutional protection over recruitment continuity.

Implement a graded response system in which minor incidents (e.g., participant disorientation lasting <5 min with full recall) are logged and discussed at a weekly safety review, while moderate or severe events (injury, persistent confusion) trigger immediate clinical assessment and conditional re-admission, balancing safety with participant retention.

Delegate incident response authority to the PI in consultation with the clinical psychologist, using case-by-case clinical judgment to distinguish parasomnia-typical behavior from concerning psychiatric symptoms, enabling rapid resolution and re-admission discussion without formal escalation protocols, accepting higher clinical decision burden in exchange for participant flexibility.
levers.review_lever: Strict protocols maximize institutional protection but risk deterring participants from returning, reducing longitudinal data richness; permissive approaches preserve enrollment but require stronger clinical judgment and peer review.

levers.name: Dual-rater scoring prioritization and inter-rater reliability reporting cadence
levers.consequences: The plan specifies that all events will be independently scored by two raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported, ensuring rigor for Aim 3 algorithm benchmarking. Choosing between real-time dual scoring (both raters independently score each night within 48 hours of capture), retrospective batch scoring (all nights scored by one rater, then a second rater re-scores 20–30% for reliability auditing), or adaptive prioritization (only events flagged by the event-triage algorithm receive dual scoring) determines throughput, cost, and algorithm validation rigor. Real-time dual scoring ensures maximum data quality but creates major annotation bottleneck; batch retrospective auditing is economical but risks systematic bias if the first scorer's interpretation anchors the second; adaptive prioritization biases reliability estimates toward algorithm-flagged events.
options: Score all nights and flagged events by both raters independently in real time, with discrepancies adjudicated by a third-rater consensus process and inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) reported monthly by event type, ensuring maximum rigor but requiring two independent scorers working at full capacity throughout the study.

Use a single primary rater for all event scoring, then conduct a retrospective inter-rater reliability audit in which a second rater independently re-scores a randomly stratified 25% sample of nights (ensuring representation across participants, event types, and study phases) with annual kappa reporting, reducing labor cost but accepting higher risk of systematic first-rater bias.

Implement adaptive dual scoring in which all participant baseline nights and nights with algorithm-flagged events receive real-time dual scoring, while non-flagged routine nights are scored by a single rater and then spot-checked at 10% frequency, optimizing scoring resource allocation toward high-information events but biasing inter-rater reliability estimates upward.
levers.review_lever: Real-time dual scoring maximizes rigor but creates unsustainable annotation labor; batch auditing and adaptive approaches reduce cost but introduce systematic bias or selective reliability reporting.

levers.name: University Hospital affiliation leverage and clinical referral sustainability
levers.consequences: The facility relies on referrals from the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologists, and the national sleep medicine society network to sustain recruitment. Choosing between tight institutional integration (formal beds or clinic slots reserved within the hospital, formal referral SLAs), arm's-length collaboration (loose referral agreements with no explicit slot guarantees), or diversified recruitment (active outreach to patient advocacy organizations, general practitioners, online screening portals) determines recruitment pipeline stability but affects institutional resource claims, independence, and reputational exposure. Tight integration secures referral volume but cedes operational autonomy and may create scheduling conflicts; loose partnerships minimize constraints but leave enrollment vulnerable to competing hospital priorities or provider turnover.
options: Negotiate a formal service-level agreement with the University Hospital sleep clinic establishing a minimum monthly referral target, reserved clinic slots for pre-admission screening, and joint publication on facility operations and safety outcomes, binding the hospital's institutional reputation to the facility's success and securing dedicated referral flow.

Maintain an arm's-length referral arrangement with University Hospital and regional neurologists using informal networks and annual stakeholder meetings, supplemented by independent recruitment advertising through the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin and direct outreach to general practitioners, minimizing institutional constraints but accepting higher recruitment volatility.

Establish a formal patient-centered recruitment channel via partnership with a German parasomnia patient advocacy organization or online sleep medicine community, embedding facility information in patient education materials and enabling self-referral, diversifying recruitment sources but introducing new consent and safety-screening overhead.
levers.review_lever: Formal hospital integration secures referrals but creates operational dependencies and shared reputational risk; arm's-length and patient-centered strategies offer independence but leave enrollment vulnerable to market fluctuations.

levers.name: Enhanced-night PSG scheduling and comparative polysomnography yield
levers.consequences: The plan schedules enhanced-night PSG montage (standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, leg EMG) only on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant, balancing physiological depth against equipment time and technician setup burden. Choosing between universal enhanced-night PSG (every night for all participants, maximizing event resolution), event-triggered escalation only (enhanced PSG deployed after technician-flagged events on dry-electrode nights), or random sampling (enhanced PSG on 20–30% of nights across the cohort regardless of flags) shapes the sensitivity of the event-triage algorithm to classical PSG versus dry-electrode EEG signals but creates different equipment utilization and comparative rigor profiles.
options: Deploy enhanced PSG montage only after technician-identified events on dry-electrode nights, supplemented by mandatory PSG on the first, mid-stay, and final nights per protocol, concentrating advanced sensing on high-yield moments and reserving PSG equipment for escalation, minimizing setup burden but creating selection bias toward technician-detected events in algorithm training data.

Implement random stratified enhanced-night PSG in which 25% of all nights across all participants receive full PSG montage (stratified by study phase and participant recruitment order) independent of technician flags, enabling unbiased comparison of dry-electrode versus standard PSG signal morphology and providing algorithm training data on both flagged and unflagged nights.

Expand the enhanced-night schedule to include PSG on every second or third night of each participant's stay, providing denser coverage of event morphology variability and increasing the probability of capturing a parasomnia event at clinical-grade resolution, accepting higher equipment and technician workload but improving algorithm training data richness.
levers.review_lever: Event-triggered PSG maximizes equipment efficiency but biases algorithm training toward technician-detected patterns; random sampling ensures unbiased comparison but increases PSG logistical burden without guaranteeing event coverage.

levers.name: Year-two funding contingency and external grant diversification strategy
levers.consequences: Year-three operations are conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24; success criteria include enrollment of 50–70 participants and capture of a prespecified minimum number of adjudicated events. However, the funding timeline assumes DFG grant and University of Bonn internal funding as primary pillars, with pharmaceutical industry partnership framed as optional upside. Choosing between aggressive early pursuit of pharma partnership to lock in year-three certainty, diversified grant applications to German research foundations and EU horizon programs, or deferred grant strategy (completing Aim 1 and Aim 2 with existing funds before seeking expansion funding) determines financial runway, institutional autonomy, and grant-writing overhead during critical operational phases. Pharma partnerships accelerate funding security but introduce publication-review processes and potential perception of bias; multiple grant applications distribute risk but require substantial proposal effort; deferred strategy preserves independence but risks operational pause if year-two progress is marginal.
options: Initiate active negotiations with pharmaceutical partners during year one, structuring a three-year contract covering year-three operations and year-two algorithm development with publication rights reserved but pre-publication review windows honored, providing funding certainty by month 12 but requiring partnership governance and stakeholder management from the outset.

Submit parallel grant applications to the German Research Foundation (DFG), EU Horizon Europe sleep and neuroscience programs, and German patient foundation funding bodies by month 12, targeting year-three and post-project funding with diversified portfolio strategy, maximizing potential funding sources but creating sustained proposal-writing burden during year-one facility setup.

Execute a self-contained year-one and year-two operational plan funded by existing DFG and university funding, defer industry or new-grant pursuit until month 20–24 when Aim 1 results and preliminary participant cohort data are available for stronger grant narratives, accepting year-three funding uncertainty but preserving full academic independence and allowing strategic partnership decisions based on emerging facility needs.
levers.review_lever: Pharma partnerships ensure year-three funding but introduce governance and publication-review overhead; diversified grants reduce funding risk but multiply proposal burden; deferred strategy preserves autonomy but leaves operations vulnerable to year-three funding gaps if month-24 progress is modest.

responses.strategic_rationale: This parasomnia research unit faces three core tensions: (1) capturing rare, naturalistic events requires long residential stays and sensitive instrumentation, but prolonged occupancy inflates per-participant cost and staffing complexity; (2) rigorous event annotation demands dual-rater consensus and physiological detail, yet manual scoring becomes a bottleneck as event volume grows; (3) early-stage methodological validation must demonstrate safe operations and publishable phenotyping, but regulatory constraints, participant exclusion criteria, and facility safety thresholds create hard operational ceilings that constrain enrollment velocity. The levers below target these three trade-offs by decoupling decisions about stay duration, scoring architecture, and safety thresholds — allowing the team to navigate speed-versus-quality, cost-versus-yield, and methodological rigor-versus-feasibility without abandoning the core residential model.

levers.name: Participant stay duration boundaries and event-yield threshold
levers.consequences: Shorter target stays (e.g., 2–3 weeks fixed) reduce facility occupancy overhead and participant dropout risk but may miss low-frequency events and force early discharge of non-productive admissions. Longer stays (up to the current 10-week ceiling) increase event capture probability and within-person pattern characterization, but compound staffing scheduling, meal provision, and per-participant cost per event ultimately captured.
options: Set a rigid 14-day minimum stay for all participants to standardize occupancy planning and simplify technician shift scheduling, with extension only after documented zero-event week.

Adopt a dynamic stay model where stay length is negotiated in week one based on observed event frequency and participant tolerability, with explicit exit criteria (two consecutive event-free weeks) rather than a fixed ceiling.

Implement a tiered stay protocol: 10 days baseline for all, then automatic 7-day extension for any participant producing fewer than one captured event, capped at 24 days total to maintain predictable bed turnover.
levers.review_lever: Shorter stays reduce cost per bed-night but increase the proportion of admissions that fail to yield any event, triggering costly protocol extensions; longer stays capture more within-person patterns but amplify scheduling complexity. None of the three options address the trade-off between cost-per-event-captured and statistical power from repeated sampling within the same individual.

levers.name: Mattress-sensor sensitivity tuning and movement-detection false-alarm rate
levers.consequences: Higher sensitivity in contact-free mattress sensors detects more subtle nocturnal movements and arousals, reducing the risk of missing a parasomnia event, but generates more false alarms that require technician review and video confirmation, consuming annotation time. Lower sensitivity reduces false alarms and technician workload but risks missing low-amplitude events or events in participants with atypical sleep postures.
options: Calibrate mattress sensors at a permissive threshold (high sensitivity) during month one to establish the false-alarm baseline and characterize noise patterns, then post-hoc filter alerts using machine-learning classifiers trained on annotated month-one data before applying to subsequent cohorts.

Set a conservative baseline sensitivity across all participants based on pre-study bench testing with expected motion ranges in normal sleep, accepting a measured false-alarm rate of 5–10% per night as acceptable technician overhead.

Deploy a participant-adaptive sensitivity model in which each individual's mattress threshold is re-tuned after the first 3 nights based on their own resting heart rate, sleep architecture, and observed movement amplitude, then locked for the remainder of their stay.
levers.review_lever: Overly sensitive detection floods the technician with low-priority alerts; overly conservative thresholds risk missing clinically significant events. All three options defer the core trade-off: whether false-alarm burden should be front-loaded (calibration phase) or spread evenly (tolerable baseline) or individualized at the cost of additional setup complexity.

levers.name: Enhanced-night PSG scheduling frequency and polysomnography resource allocation
levers.consequences: More frequent enhanced nights (e.g., every 3–4 days rather than first, mid-stay, and final) improve granular physiological characterization and increase the probability of PSG coinciding with a parasomnia event, but consume equipment hours, technician setup time, and budget rapidly. Fewer enhanced nights reduce operational burden and costs but may miss rare events and provide sparse longitudinal physiology coverage.
options: Schedule enhanced PSG on a fixed calendar (every fourth night) regardless of event detection, ensuring even temporal spacing and predictable technician workload, with explicit participant notification at admission.

Concentrate enhanced nights only after a mattress-sensor or video-detected event alert within the prior 24 hours, plus routine nights on admission and discharge, to align expensive PSG with probable event windows.

Randomize enhanced-night scheduling across participants and weeks using a stratified design, with 30% of study nights receiving full PSG, ensuring statistical comparability of enhanced versus routine nights without clustering bias.
levers.review_lever: Fixed schedules are operationally simple but wasteful if events cluster; event-triggered scheduling conserves resources but misses asymptomatic nights and skews the cohort towards detected-event participants. Random scheduling adds complexity for minimal scientific gain in a methods-validation study.

levers.name: Dual-rater scoring workflow and inter-rater agreement enforcement
levers.consequences: Independent scoring of all events by two raters ensures robust consensus and published inter-rater reliability metrics required for methodological credibility. Adjudication of disagreements adds a third-rater step or PI arbitration, strengthening the final dataset but increasing per-event review time and cost. Conversely, accepting a lower agreement threshold (e.g., 80% IRA instead of 95%) speeds publication but invites criticism of loose event definition.
options: Require consensus on all scored events via a mandatory three-rater adjudication protocol in which a senior sleep neurophysiologist breaks all rater disagreements before any event is labeled 'adjudicated,' with agreement and tie-breaking rules documented prospectively.

Deploy a two-rater model with pre-agreed AASM criteria and no third-rater arbitration; report inter-rater reliability openly (e.g., Cohen's kappa, percentage agreement) and use only events with ≥90% IRA for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis.

Implement rolling single-rater scoring for screening events (initial triage), with dual-rater review reserved for a stratified subsample (20% of all nights) plus all events flagged by the primary rater as 'borderline or equivocal,' balancing thoroughness with throughput.
levers.review_lever: Mandatory consensus ensures defensible event labels but consumes rater time; two-rater agreement with transparency is faster but risks weaker inter-rater metrics; selective dual-rating is cost-efficient but introduces sampling bias if not stratified carefully.

levers.name: Residential environment domesticity versus clinical monitoring visibility
levers.consequences: A genuinely residential aesthetic (subdued lighting, home furniture, minimal visible sensors, private bedrooms) encourages naturalistic sleep and parasomnia expression, aligning with the stated goal of capturing behavior in domestic-like contexts. Increased clinical visibility (visible EEG leads, obvious cameras, clinical-grade bedside monitors) reassures safety monitoring and regulatory inspectors but may suppress natural sleep patterns and increase participant anxiety, potentially reducing parasomnia event frequency.
options: Design bedrooms with concealed or cosmetically integrated sensors (recessed camera domes, fabric-friendly electrode patches, under-bed mattress sensors), muted color schemes, and household-style furnishings, with a separate clinical observation room for technicians and monitors located outside the sleeping area.

Adopt a hybrid layout with a prominent bedside safety station (visible monitor, call button, technician intercom) at the foot of each bed paired with decorative lighting and residential furniture, signaling safety preparedness while maintaining a sleep-conducive environment.

Construct a fully clinical-grade monitoring suite with standard hospital beds, continuous visible telemetry, overhead EEG lead racks, and integrated camera housings, accepting reduced environmental domesticity in exchange for unambiguous regulatory compliance and technician situational awareness.
levers.review_lever: Disguised sensors maximize behavioral naturalism but complicate troubleshooting and regulatory documentation; visible clinical infrastructure ensures safety clarity but risks suppressing the parasomnia expression the study aims to capture.

levers.name: Semi-automated event-triage algorithm training data and algorithm-rater comparison strategy
levers.consequences: Training the triage algorithm on a large in-house annotated dataset (e.g., first 6 months of dual-rated events) improves domain specificity and sensitivity to the facility's sensor characteristics, but delays algorithm deployment and requires in-house labeling labor. Using a smaller training set or external benchmark data accelerates triage deployment but risks poor generalization to local sensor noise and participant movement patterns.
options: Reserve the first 100 captured and adjudicated events (regardless of how many months this requires) as a held-out test set; train the algorithm on all subsequent events, enabling evaluation of algorithmic sensitivity and specificity against dual human raters on truly independent data.

Prospectively designate 40% of study nights for algorithm training (manually scored by two raters) and 60% for algorithm evaluation, stratified by participant, to balance training-set size with statistical power for the final sensitivity-specificity report.

Collaborate with an external computational sleep lab to pre-train the algorithm on a published multi-center parasomnia EEG dataset, then fine-tune on the first 50 local events, reducing in-house annotation burden while retaining local calibration.
levers.review_lever: Large in-house training delays deployment and consumes rater time; small training sets or external pre-training risks poor local generalization; stratified train-test designs solve the evaluation trade-off but require prospective commitment to reduced in-house algorithm iteration.

levers.name: Matched control participant recruitment source and baseline behavioral characterization
levers.consequences: Recruiting healthy controls from the general population (via advertisement or volunteer registries) provides a true baseline for non-parasomnia nocturnal behavior and sensor false-positive rates, but requires independent screening, consent, and compensation for individuals with no clinical referral pathway. Recruiting controls from the sleep clinic (e.g., individuals evaluated for insomnia or mild sleep apnea but not meeting exclusion criteria) shortens recruitment timeline and leverages existing patient relationships, but introduces subtle confounding if controls differ systematically in age, comorbidity, or familiarity with sleep medicine.
options: Recruit all controls through open community advertisement with a streamlined health-history questionnaire and phone screening, targeting age-matched and sex-matched pairing with the parasomnia cohort, accepting lower conversion rates to maximize independence.

Partner with the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic to enroll controls from a standing pool of polysomnography wait-list patients who have been clinically cleared and are willing to participate in research, reducing recruitment lag.

Use a convenience-sampling approach: recruit controls from hospital and university staff and their households, offering the same €80-per-night compensation, with explicit documentation of occupation and any self-reported sleep complaints to control for confounding in the analysis.
levers.review_lever: Community recruitment ensures independence but is slower and costlier; clinic-based controls are faster but risk subtle clinical confounding; convenience sampling is fastest but introduces institutional-affiliation bias into the baseline dataset.

levers.name: Recruitment pathway stringency and bed-partner corroboration
levers.consequences: Stricter pre-admission clinical assessment and mandatory bed-partner history validation reduce enrollment velocity but increase likelihood that admitted participants actually produce parasomnia events during their stay, raising event-capture yield and reducing unproductive admissions. Conversely, looser intake criteria accelerate participant throughput but risk admitting non-event-producing individuals who consume facility time and staff attention without contributing to Aim 2 phenotyping or Aim 3 algorithm benchmarking.
options: Require prospective event logs and actigraphy tracings for 4 weeks prior to admission, with bed-partner structured interview conducted by the clinical psychologist before consent, adjudicated by the PI to confirm ≥2 episodes per month with documented witness accounts

Implement single-night screening polysomnography in the university hospital sleep lab before residential unit admission, using standard AASM criteria to confirm parasomnia events or high-arousal burden, accepting longer pre-admission latency but filtering out misdiagnosed referrals

Accept specialist clinical referral and patient self-report with brief telephone bed-partner screening, prioritizing enrollment speed over pre-admission event confirmation and tolerating a higher proportion of non-productive admissions that trigger extended-stay protocols or contribute to the 20% unproductive threshold
levers.review: Stricter screening slows enrollment but increases event yield; looser screening sacrifices yield for speed — the options do not address how to recover lost participants if screening backlog exceeds PI capacity or if regional referral networks deplete before enrollment targets are reached.

levers.name: Night technician staffing model and shift coverage
levers.consequences: The current plan deploys 3 technicians rotating night shifts to cover 8 active suites. A dedicated 4-person roster with overlap increases margin for event response, real-time annotation accuracy, and staff fatigue management, but adds €80K–€120K annually in salaries plus social insurance. Conversely, outsourcing night coverage to a contracted nursing agency trades salary burden for reduced control over annotation quality, event-flagging consistency, and participant relationship continuity.
options: Hire a fourth technician to implement a 4-on-3-off rotating roster with one technician free for ad-hoc escalation or annotation spillover, absorbing the additional cost as a priority within personnel budget to sustain annotation throughput and participant safety margins at full 8-suite capacity

Negotiate a contracted night-nursing partnership with a local Bonn agency under a protocol-specific training agreement, where agency staff complete a 2-week facility orientation and follow standardized event-flagging and annotation workflows, reducing fixed payroll but introducing turnover risk and potential annotation drift

Operate the 3-person roster at full capacity with a documented protocol ceiling of 6 active suites at any time to manage technician workload within safe limits, accepting slower enrollment velocity and longer study duration but avoiding overstaffing cost if participant recruitment remains below target.
levers.review: Hiring a fourth technician secures annotation quality and safety margin but locks in fixed cost; outsourcing reduces payroll but risks annotation drift; capping suites at 6 avoids overstaffing cost but conflicts with the 50–70 participant enrollment target if sustained recruitment exceeds 6-suite capacity.

levers.name: Dry-electrode EEG headband reliability and backup sensing strategy
levers.consequences: The tiered acquisition model uses dry-electrode EEG headbands for nightly low-burden monitoring, reducing participant discomfort and improving compliance, but dry-electrode contact quality degrades over multi-week stays and can produce motion artifacts during parasomnia events. A contingency strategy — such as maintaining a spare headband inventory and training technicians in real-time contact troubleshooting — mitigates data-loss risk but requires procedural discipline. Relying entirely on scheduled enhanced-night PSG (first, mid, final nights) as backup may miss events occurring on other nights.
options: Stock a 2-week rotating spare headband inventory with standardized contact-gel resupply and train technicians to perform contact-quality checks and in-situ electrode replacement during each morning review window, treating headband maintenance as a core daily task and budgeting for incremental gel and replacement-electrode costs

Deploy full standard scalp EEG (10–20 system) every night rather than reserving it for enhanced nights, accepting increased setup labor and participant discomfort but eliminating the risk that infrequent events on non-enhanced nights are captured only by low-resolution contact-free sensors

Use dry-electrode headbands nightly with no backup EEG on non-enhanced nights, relying on contact-free mattress sensors, infrared video, and microphone data to detect parasomnia episodes and escalate to full PSG setup after technician-flagged events, accepting the tradeoff that initial event morphology on non-enhanced nights remains low-resolution unless escalation occurs.
levers.review: Headband maintenance adds procedural overhead and consumable cost; nightly full scalp EEG increases setup labor and participant burden; pure low-resolution reliance gambles on escalation-flag accuracy — none address how to recover or retrospectively analyze morphology if a headband fails mid-event on a non-enhanced night.

levers.name: Event-triage algorithm development scope and human-scorer dependency
levers.consequences: The plan commits to semi-automated event-triage tools benchmarked against dual human scorer agreement, reducing manual review burden (Aim 3) while preserving clinical rigor. Expanding the algorithm to autonomously diagnose parasomnia subtype (sleepwalking vs. terror vs. confusional arousal) requires larger training datasets and validation complexity, risking missed publication deadline if algorithm development extends into year three. Conversely, limiting the algorithm to event-presence detection only (binary: parasomnia vs. background motion) reduces development scope but provides less actionable output for clinical phenotyping.
options: Scope the algorithm to detect parasomnia event windows and rank confidence, leaving human scorers to classify subtype and morphology, completing algorithm benchmarking by month 24 and publishing Aim 3 results within the grant timeline

Design the algorithm to classify NREM parasomnia subtype (sleepwalking vs. confusional arousal vs. terror) using multi-modal sensor features and video motion signatures, accepting extended development timeline and deferring final benchmarking to month 30–32 with Aim 3 publication contingent on timely data accumulation

Restrict the algorithm to detecting gross nocturnal movement above a static threshold (e.g., mattress pressure and video motion exceeding baseline), deliberately avoiding subtype classification or morphological analysis, completing a lightweight tool by month 18 that supports technician workflow but offers minimal novel scientific content for publication.
levers.review: Full subtype classification risks timeline slippage; binary detection alone limits publication novelty; hybrid scope still requires dual human scoring for algorithm ground truth, leaving the resource burden of training and retaining two independent raters unaddressed.

levers.name: Matched control cohort size and recruitment source
levers.consequences: The plan includes a matched control group to benchmark sensor false-positive rates and normal nocturnal movement patterns. Recruiting 20–25 matched controls (matched on age, sex, BMI) in parallel with patient enrollment provides robust baselines for Aim 3 algorithm specificity. Conversely, recruiting controls sequentially after patient enrollment completes eliminates resource contention but delays algorithm validation. Recruiting controls from the general population (e.g., via university advertisement) is faster than recruiting from the hospital but may miss sleep-clinic workers or staff who have high familiarity with the facility and atypical sleep patterns.
options: Enroll 20–25 matched controls on the same recruitment timeline as parasomnia patients, assigning controls to 1–2 dedicated suite rotations per month and training technicians in control-specific workflows (shorter stays, simpler consent, absence of event-escalation protocols), to complete algorithm specificity benchmarking in parallel with patient data collection

Recruit matched controls exclusively from University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic staff and immediate family members, leveraging convenience sampling and pre-existing trust but accepting potential bias if clinic workers have altered sleep physiology due to occupational stress or shift work history

Defer control recruitment to months 28–32 after achieving the target 50–70 parasomnia participants, allowing full focus on event capture during the main study window and performing algorithm specificity analysis in a compressed timeline with parallel control stays.
levers.review: Parallel control enrollment adds recruitment burden and suite allocation pressure during year one; convenience sampling from clinic staff risks physiological bias; deferring controls simplifies year-one operations but compresses algorithm validation into months 28–32, creating timeline risk if data quality review or rater retraining is needed.

levers.name: Data sharing repository selection and privacy-constraint communication
levers.consequences: The plan designates public data sharing to de-identified physiological and sensor data only, excluding bedroom video due to privacy constraints. Depositing data in a specialized sleep-research repository (e.g., NATDB, OpenNeuro, SleepData.org) maximizes discoverability and reproducibility but requires BIDS compliance enforcement and licensing agreements negotiation. Alternatively, restricting data sharing to collaborator-requested access under formal data use agreements reduces public burden but limits discoverability and reproducibility. Clear communication to participants about video-non-sharing increases trust and consent robustness.
options: Commit to depositing de-identified polysomnography, dry-electrode headband, mattress-sensor, and environmental-sensor streams in OpenNeuro Sleep using EEG-BIDS formatting, with dual-anonymization (remove dates, replace identifiers) and automatic flagging of video-containing sessions as excluded from deposition, completing deposit within 3 months of final publication to maximize discoverability

Implement a restricted-access model where polysomnography and sensor data are shared only to qualified sleep researchers under formal data use agreements signed with the university legal office, allowing fine-grained control over reuse but requiring a data-sharing coordinator role and accepting reduced public impact compared to open-repository deposition

Create a study-specific data portal hosted on University of Bonn servers with conditional access to de-identified streams, where external researchers submit a research proposal and gain access within 2 weeks if approved by the PI, striking a middle ground between discoverability and privacy control but introducing administrative overhead and portal maintenance.
levers.review: OpenNeuro deposition maximizes reproducibility but requires strict BIDS compliance and early commitment; restricted data-use agreements preserve privacy control but require dedicated coordination; a university portal balances control and access but depends on sustained IT infrastructure and governance, leaving the long-term maintenance burden unspecified.

levers.name: Year-two expansion decision trigger and facility utilization threshold
levers.consequences: The plan defers 4-suite expansion (from 8 to 12 active suites) until pilot data confirms acceptable data quality, false-alarm rates, and staffing safety by the end of year one. Expanding early maximizes enrollment velocity and event-yield accumulation toward the 50–70 target, but risks operational chaos if staffing or annotation infrastructure is unprepared. Deferring expansion entirely protects year-two cash flow and reduces risk of over-capacity chaos, but may result in undershoot of enrollment targets if year-one recruitment outpaces pilot projections.
options: Trigger expansion to 12 suites in month 13 if year-one data achieves ≥80% suite utilization (i.e., ≥6.4 suites occupied on average), ≥70% event-capture rate (participants producing ≥1 adjudicated event), and inter-rater reliability ≥0.75 kappa for parasomnia event classification, with facility director and external SAB approval required before hiring expansion staff

Commit to 8-suite cap through month 24 regardless of year-one recruitment success, prioritizing operational stability and staff learning-curve maturation over enrollment velocity, with a formal go/no-go review in month 20 assessing whether event-yield and publication progress warrant expansion planning for month 25 onward

Conduct a month-12 capacity utilization audit and automatically scale staffing (but not physical suites) to 4-person technician roster and enhanced-night PSG frequency if average suite occupancy exceeds 7 suites, deferring physical suite expansion until month 18 when renovations can be planned and contracted, maintaining flexibility while protecting year-one operations.
levers.review: Quantitative expansion triggers reduce subjective decision-making but assume month-13 staffing availability and reinforce suite-utilization dependency; 8-suite cap prioritizes stability but risks enrollment shortfall if word-of-mouth recruitment accelerates; scaled staffing without suite expansion buys time but still commits to additional hiring before physical expansion certainty.

levers.name: Participant dwell-time architecture and re-admission protocols
levers.consequences: Choosing between longer single stays (2–8 weeks, or extended to 10 weeks for zero-event cases) versus repeated shorter admissions (e.g., two 2-week stays separated by months) directly affects event capture likelihood but creates different staffing load curves and participant burden. Longer stays may improve within-person temporal clustering detection but increase accommodation risk; shorter repeated stays distribute risk but require re-consent, re-baseline, and repeated technician orientation, multiplying annotation overhead.
options: Implement a fixed 4-week baseline stay for all participants with a structured optional second admission triggered only if zero events are captured during the first stay, capping total facility exposure time per participant at 8 weeks and creating a stable scheduling pattern.

Deploy an adaptive stay-length model in which initial stay duration (2–5 weeks) is set by the PI after pre-admission assessment of episode frequency history, with post-stay event-count data driving individual re-admission decisions within the 10-week ceiling, optimizing for high event-yield per participant but requiring continuous real-time scheduling recalculation.

Offer all participants a structured three-visit protocol of two separate 2-week admissions separated by 4–6 weeks at home, bookended by a final 1-week validation stay, enabling longitudinal within-person variance assessment and comparison of home versus residential capture but requiring tripled consent and technician cross-training cycles.
levers.review: Longer stays improve event capture per admission but create seasonal staffing peaks and participant fatigue-driven safety risks; shorter repeated stays distribute load but triple administrative overhead and inter-rater consistency challenges across separate baseline periods.

levers.name: Technician shift-rotation stability and on-call surge capacity
levers.consequences: The unit currently plans 3 rotating technicians covering 8 active suites per night with margin for event response and real-time annotation. Choosing between a fixed roster of permanent full-time technicians versus a hybrid model mixing core staff with per-shift on-call contractors or regional sleep center partnerships determines long-term cost stability, annotation consistency, and continuity of participant safety protocols. Permanent staff ensures protocol fidelity and builds institutional memory but locks in fixed wages; hybrid models provide budget flexibility and surge capacity for year-two expansion but introduce training variability and annotation drift.
options: Maintain a stable core of 3 full-time permanent technicians supplemented by a pre-qualified on-call freelance pool from regional sleep centers, staggered to cover unplanned absences and participant surges, with quarterly cross-training sessions and spot-check dual-annotation alignment audits.

Hire 4 permanent full-time technicians from year one, creating intentional redundancy for participant safety and enabling one dedicated technician per 2 suites on each shift, accepting higher baseline labor costs but achieving superior continuity of scoring methodology and participant rapport.

Contract with a specialized overnight staffing agency to supply technicians on a per-shift basis, supplemented by a single dedicated full-time facility manager who orients each temporary technician and audits annotation quality, minimizing facility fixed costs but outsourcing consistency and requiring robust quality-control infrastructure.
levers.review: Permanent staff ensures consistency but locks in fixed wages regardless of utilization; hybrid and agency models trade flexibility for training overhead and inter-rater drift that compounds annotation bottlenecks.

levers.name: Facility safety-incident response threshold and escalation authority
levers.consequences: Adults with parasomnia carry inherent nocturnal movement and confusion risk—the facility design mitigates via padded corridors and door alarms, but decisions about when to restrict admissions, call emergency services, extend monitoring, or exclude participants from further stays shape both safety perception and recruitment continuity. A strict incident-response protocol with low thresholds (e.g., immediate psychiatric consultation after any participant confusion or injury, mandatory emergency department evaluation) protects liability but may deter participant re-admission and create false-positive safety exclusions; permissive thresholds maximize enrollment but increase reputational and medical risk.
options: Establish a strict incident-escalation protocol requiring immediate notification to the clinical psychologist, documentation in a safety event log, and structured psychiatric clearance or exclusion before any participant returns for a subsequent stay, prioritizing transparency and institutional protection over recruitment continuity.

Implement a graded response system in which minor incidents (e.g., participant disorientation lasting <5 min with full recall) are logged and discussed at a weekly safety review, while moderate or severe events (injury, persistent confusion) trigger immediate clinical assessment and conditional re-admission, balancing safety with participant retention.

Delegate incident response authority to the PI in consultation with the clinical psychologist, using case-by-case clinical judgment to distinguish parasomnia-typical behavior from concerning psychiatric symptoms, enabling rapid resolution and re-admission discussion without formal escalation protocols, accepting higher clinical decision burden in exchange for participant flexibility.
levers.review: Strict protocols maximize institutional protection but risk deterring participants from returning, reducing longitudinal data richness; permissive approaches preserve enrollment but require stronger clinical judgment and peer review.

levers.name: Dual-rater scoring prioritization and inter-rater reliability reporting cadence
levers.consequences: The plan specifies that all events will be independently scored by two raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported, ensuring rigor for Aim 3 algorithm benchmarking. Choosing between real-time dual scoring (both raters independently score each night within 48 hours of capture), retrospective batch scoring (all nights scored by one rater, then a second rater re-scores 20–30% for reliability auditing), or adaptive prioritization (only events flagged by the event-triage algorithm receive dual scoring) determines throughput, cost, and algorithm validation rigor. Real-time dual scoring ensures maximum data quality but creates major annotation bottleneck; batch retrospective auditing is economical but risks systematic bias if the first scorer's interpretation anchors the second; adaptive prioritization biases reliability estimates toward algorithm-flagged events.
options: Score all nights and flagged events by both raters independently in real time, with discrepancies adjudicated by a third-rater consensus process and inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) reported monthly by event type, ensuring maximum rigor but requiring two independent scorers working at full capacity throughout the study.

Use a single primary rater for all event scoring, then conduct a retrospective inter-rater reliability audit in which a second rater independently re-scores a randomly stratified 25% sample of nights (ensuring representation across participants, event types, and study phases) with annual kappa reporting, reducing labor cost but accepting higher risk of systematic first-rater bias.

Implement adaptive dual scoring in which all participant baseline nights and nights with algorithm-flagged events receive real-time dual scoring, while non-flagged routine nights are scored by a single rater and then spot-checked at 10% frequency, optimizing scoring resource allocation toward high-information events but biasing inter-rater reliability estimates upward.
levers.review: Real-time dual scoring maximizes rigor but creates unsustainable annotation labor; batch auditing and adaptive approaches reduce cost but introduce systematic bias or selective reliability reporting.

levers.name: University Hospital affiliation leverage and clinical referral sustainability
levers.consequences: The facility relies on referrals from the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologists, and the national sleep medicine society network to sustain recruitment. Choosing between tight institutional integration (formal beds or clinic slots reserved within the hospital, formal referral SLAs), arm's-length collaboration (loose referral agreements with no explicit slot guarantees), or diversified recruitment (active outreach to patient advocacy organizations, general practitioners, online screening portals) determines recruitment pipeline stability but affects institutional resource claims, independence, and reputational exposure. Tight integration secures referral volume but cedes operational autonomy and may create scheduling conflicts; loose partnerships minimize constraints but leave enrollment vulnerable to competing hospital priorities or provider turnover.
options: Negotiate a formal service-level agreement with the University Hospital sleep clinic establishing a minimum monthly referral target, reserved clinic slots for pre-admission screening, and joint publication on facility operations and safety outcomes, binding the hospital's institutional reputation to the facility's success and securing dedicated referral flow.

Maintain an arm's-length referral arrangement with University Hospital and regional neurologists using informal networks and annual stakeholder meetings, supplemented by independent recruitment advertising through the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin and direct outreach to general practitioners, minimizing institutional constraints but accepting higher recruitment volatility.

Establish a formal patient-centered recruitment channel via partnership with a German parasomnia patient advocacy organization or online sleep medicine community, embedding facility information in patient education materials and enabling self-referral, diversifying recruitment sources but introducing new consent and safety-screening overhead.
levers.review: Formal hospital integration secures referrals but creates operational dependencies and shared reputational risk; arm's-length and patient-centered strategies offer independence but leave enrollment vulnerable to market fluctuations.

levers.name: Enhanced-night PSG scheduling and comparative polysomnography yield
levers.consequences: The plan schedules enhanced-night PSG montage (standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, leg EMG) only on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant, balancing physiological depth against equipment time and technician setup burden. Choosing between universal enhanced-night PSG (every night for all participants, maximizing event resolution), event-triggered escalation only (enhanced PSG deployed after technician-flagged events on dry-electrode nights), or random sampling (enhanced PSG on 20–30% of nights across the cohort regardless of flags) shapes the sensitivity of the event-triage algorithm to classical PSG versus dry-electrode EEG signals but creates different equipment utilization and comparative rigor profiles.
options: Deploy enhanced PSG montage only after technician-identified events on dry-electrode nights, supplemented by mandatory PSG on the first, mid-stay, and final nights per protocol, concentrating advanced sensing on high-yield moments and reserving PSG equipment for escalation, minimizing setup burden but creating selection bias toward technician-detected events in algorithm training data.

Implement random stratified enhanced-night PSG in which 25% of all nights across all participants receive full PSG montage (stratified by study phase and participant recruitment order) independent of technician flags, enabling unbiased comparison of dry-electrode versus standard PSG signal morphology and providing algorithm training data on both flagged and unflagged nights.

Expand the enhanced-night schedule to include PSG on every second or third night of each participant's stay, providing denser coverage of event morphology variability and increasing the probability of capturing a parasomnia event at clinical-grade resolution, accepting higher equipment and technician workload but improving algorithm training data richness.
levers.review: Event-triggered PSG maximizes equipment efficiency but biases algorithm training toward technician-detected patterns; random sampling ensures unbiased comparison but increases PSG logistical burden without guaranteeing event coverage.

levers.name: Year-two funding contingency and external grant diversification strategy
levers.consequences: Year-three operations are conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24; success criteria include enrollment of 50–70 participants and capture of a prespecified minimum number of adjudicated events. However, the funding timeline assumes DFG grant and University of Bonn internal funding as primary pillars, with pharmaceutical industry partnership framed as optional upside. Choosing between aggressive early pursuit of pharma partnership to lock in year-three certainty, diversified grant applications to German research foundations and EU horizon programs, or deferred grant strategy (completing Aim 1 and Aim 2 with existing funds before seeking expansion funding) determines financial runway, institutional autonomy, and grant-writing overhead during critical operational phases. Pharma partnerships accelerate funding security but introduce publication-review processes and potential perception of bias; multiple grant applications distribute risk but require substantial proposal effort; deferred strategy preserves independence but risks operational pause if year-two progress is marginal.
options: Initiate active negotiations with pharmaceutical partners during year one, structuring a three-year contract covering year-three operations and year-two algorithm development with publication rights reserved but pre-publication review windows honored, providing funding certainty by month 12 but requiring partnership governance and stakeholder management from the outset.

Submit parallel grant applications to the German Research Foundation (DFG), EU Horizon Europe sleep and neuroscience programs, and German patient foundation funding bodies by month 12, targeting year-three and post-project funding with diversified portfolio strategy, maximizing potential funding sources but creating sustained proposal-writing burden during year-one facility setup.

Execute a self-contained year-one and year-two operational plan funded by existing DFG and university funding, defer industry or new-grant pursuit until month 20–24 when Aim 1 results and preliminary participant cohort data are available for stronger grant narratives, accepting year-three funding uncertainty but preserving full academic independence and allowing strategic partnership decisions based on emerging facility needs.
levers.review: Pharma partnerships ensure year-three funding but introduce governance and publication-review overhead; diversified grants reduce funding risk but multiply proposal burden; deferred strategy preserves autonomy but leaves operations vulnerable to year-three funding gaps if month-24 progress is modest.

levers.name: Participant stay duration boundaries and event-yield threshold
levers.consequences: Shorter target stays (e.g., 2–3 weeks fixed) reduce facility occupancy overhead and participant dropout risk but may miss low-frequency events and force early discharge of non-productive admissions. Longer stays (up to the current 10-week ceiling) increase event capture probability and within-person pattern characterization, but compound staffing scheduling, meal provision, and per-participant cost per event ultimately captured.
options: Set a rigid 14-day minimum stay for all participants to standardize occupancy planning and simplify technician shift scheduling, with extension only after documented zero-event week.

Adopt a dynamic stay model where stay length is negotiated in week one based on observed event frequency and participant tolerability, with explicit exit criteria (two consecutive event-free weeks) rather than a fixed ceiling.

Implement a tiered stay protocol: 10 days baseline for all, then automatic 7-day extension for any participant producing fewer than one captured event, capped at 24 days total to maintain predictable bed turnover.
levers.review: Shorter stays reduce cost per bed-night but increase the proportion of admissions that fail to yield any event, triggering costly protocol extensions; longer stays capture more within-person patterns but amplify scheduling complexity. None of the three options address the trade-off between cost-per-event-captured and statistical power from repeated sampling within the same individual.

levers.name: Mattress-sensor sensitivity tuning and movement-detection false-alarm rate
levers.consequences: Higher sensitivity in contact-free mattress sensors detects more subtle nocturnal movements and arousals, reducing the risk of missing a parasomnia event, but generates more false alarms that require technician review and video confirmation, consuming annotation time. Lower sensitivity reduces false alarms and technician workload but risks missing low-amplitude events or events in participants with atypical sleep postures.
options: Calibrate mattress sensors at a permissive threshold (high sensitivity) during month one to establish the false-alarm baseline and characterize noise patterns, then post-hoc filter alerts using machine-learning classifiers trained on annotated month-one data before applying to subsequent cohorts.

Set a conservative baseline sensitivity across all participants based on pre-study bench testing with expected motion ranges in normal sleep, accepting a measured false-alarm rate of 5–10% per night as acceptable technician overhead.

Deploy a participant-adaptive sensitivity model in which each individual's mattress threshold is re-tuned after the first 3 nights based on their own resting heart rate, sleep architecture, and observed movement amplitude, then locked for the remainder of their stay.
levers.review: Overly sensitive detection floods the technician with low-priority alerts; overly conservative thresholds risk missing clinically significant events. All three options defer the core trade-off: whether false-alarm burden should be front-loaded (calibration phase) or spread evenly (tolerable baseline) or individualized at the cost of additional setup complexity.

levers.name: Enhanced-night PSG scheduling frequency and polysomnography resource allocation
levers.consequences: More frequent enhanced nights (e.g., every 3–4 days rather than first, mid-stay, and final) improve granular physiological characterization and increase the probability of PSG coinciding with a parasomnia event, but consume equipment hours, technician setup time, and budget rapidly. Fewer enhanced nights reduce operational burden and costs but may miss rare events and provide sparse longitudinal physiology coverage.
options: Schedule enhanced PSG on a fixed calendar (every fourth night) regardless of event detection, ensuring even temporal spacing and predictable technician workload, with explicit participant notification at admission.

Concentrate enhanced nights only after a mattress-sensor or video-detected event alert within the prior 24 hours, plus routine nights on admission and discharge, to align expensive PSG with probable event windows.

Randomize enhanced-night scheduling across participants and weeks using a stratified design, with 30% of study nights receiving full PSG, ensuring statistical comparability of enhanced versus routine nights without clustering bias.
levers.review: Fixed schedules are operationally simple but wasteful if events cluster; event-triggered scheduling conserves resources but misses asymptomatic nights and skews the cohort towards detected-event participants. Random scheduling adds complexity for minimal scientific gain in a methods-validation study.

levers.name: Dual-rater scoring workflow and inter-rater agreement enforcement
levers.consequences: Independent scoring of all events by two raters ensures robust consensus and published inter-rater reliability metrics required for methodological credibility. Adjudication of disagreements adds a third-rater step or PI arbitration, strengthening the final dataset but increasing per-event review time and cost. Conversely, accepting a lower agreement threshold (e.g., 80% IRA instead of 95%) speeds publication but invites criticism of loose event definition.
options: Require consensus on all scored events via a mandatory three-rater adjudication protocol in which a senior sleep neurophysiologist breaks all rater disagreements before any event is labeled 'adjudicated,' with agreement and tie-breaking rules documented prospectively.

Deploy a two-rater model with pre-agreed AASM criteria and no third-rater arbitration; report inter-rater reliability openly (e.g., Cohen's kappa, percentage agreement) and use only events with ≥90% IRA for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis.
